summary: Proposes an elective experimental Encoding header field to allow mail with multiple parts and structures. It updates the Content-Type idea of RFC 1049 and suggests updates to the Privacy Enhancement RFCs. It was replaced by RFC 1505.

eli5.summary: A way for a letter to say what is inside and how it is packed, so the receiver can open it right.

questions: multi part email messages early proposal
subtitle: A header field for describing multi-part email messages and how to decode each part.

tldr.problem: Email messages were limited to a single body part. To send multiple items of different types in one message, there needed to be a way to describe each part and its encoding.
tldr.mechanism: The Encoding header field specifies a comma-separated list of message parts, each with a line count, a keyword naming the encoding type, and optional parameters for that type.
tldr.outcome: This allowed mail systems to handle multi-part messages with different content types and encodings, though it was later superseded by RFC 1505 which provided a more comprehensive solution.

facts.label: Number of defined encodings
facts.value: 8 (text, message, hex, evfu, edi, x.400, uuencode, encrypted)

today: RFC 1154 is an Experimental protocol from April 1990 and has been obsoleted by RFC 1505, which provided a more comprehensive solution for multi-part message handling. The concepts in 1154 contributed to the development of modern email standards for handling multiple content types and encodings.

sections.title: Multi-part Email Messages
sections.content:
RFC 822 defines email messages as having two parts: a header and a body, separated by a blank line. The Encoding header field extends this model to allow the message body to contain multiple parts, each separated from the next by a blank line.

Without the Encoding field, the message body is assumed to be a single part of type text. With it, each part can have a different encoding, allowing mail systems to transmit and properly decode binary data, structured documents, and other content types within a single message.
sections.eli5: Normally an email is like a letter: one thing with text. This RFC lets you put several different things in one envelope, each labeled with what it is.

sections.title: The Encoding Field Format
sections.content:
The Encoding field consists of one or more subfields separated by commas. Each subfield describes one message part in the order it appears in the message body.

A subfield has three components: an optional line count (a decimal number specifying the number of text lines in the part), a keyword defining the encoding type, and optional parameters specific to that encoding. The line count is required for all parts except the last one, because skipping over parts to reach a later one is faster with the count available.

Comments enclosed in parentheses can appear anywhere in the Encoding field, and mail reading systems may show them to users but must not use them for interpreting the content.
sections.eli5: Think of a label for each item: how many pages it has, what kind of thing it is, and any special instructions for opening it. The last item does not need the page count because you go through it all.

sections.title: Encoding Types
sections.content:
The RFC defines eight encoding types:

Text is the default, for message body text in ASCII or ISO 8859-1, with lines of reasonable length (under 1000 characters).

Message indicates that the body part is itself a complete Internet message with its own header and body. This is useful for resending replies and for recursively including X.400 messages.

Hex represents binary data encoded as two hexadecimal digits per byte.

EVFU (Electronic Vertical Format Unit) is a format where each line begins with a channel selector character to control printer output, sometimes called FORTRAN format.

EDI (Electronic Document Interchange) marks business documents formatted according to ANSI X12 or related standards.

X.400 provides a mapping between CCITT X.400 body parts and RFC 822 messages, either as hexadecimal-encoded X.409 or using a 3-byte to 4-character encoding.

uuencode marks sections using the output of the uuencode program from uucp.

encrypted indicates a section encrypted with methods defined in RFC 1115. Keywords beginning with X- are permanently reserved for implementation-specific use.
sections.eli5: Different types of things need different ways to pack them. Text is just words, but binary data needs hex numbers, documents need EDI format, and secret messages need encryption.

sections.title: Design Principles and Examples
sections.content:
When adding new encoding types, several principles should be followed: use the most common single-word name for the encoding, avoid overly general keywords, keep encodings free of unnecessary idiosyncrasies, and prefer 7-bit ASCII printing characters for complete transformations of a source document.

An example from the RFC illustrates a message containing a note and two X12 purchase orders with an Encoding field of: 17 TEXT, 146 EDI X12, 69 EDI X12. The first part is 17 lines of plain text, followed by two EDI parts with 146 and 69 lines respectively.

The Encoding field provides a mechanism for mapping multi-part messages between X.400 and RFC 822 formats, enabling gateways to translate between these mail systems by preserving the structure and encoding of each part.
sections.eli5: When you have a mix of things to send—a cover note, two purchase orders—you write how many lines each one is and what format it is in. That way anyone opening the mail knows exactly what they have.

sections.title: Status and Relationship to Other Standards
sections.content:
The Encoding header field was proposed as an elective experimental protocol, updating the Content-Type idea from RFC 1049. It was intended as a suggested update to the Privacy Enhancement RFCs (1113, 1114, 1115), which needed a way to handle multi-part encrypted messages.

The design intended for implementations to treat Content-Type as an alias of Encoding (when a message has only one body part), creating a unified approach to describing message structure. RFC 1154 is an Experimental status protocol from April 1990 and has been obsoleted by RFC 1505, which provided a more comprehensive and widely adopted solution for multi-part message handling.
sections.eli5: This was an early try at solving the multi-part email problem. It worked, but later versions did it better and became the standard everyone uses.
